chapter: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
title: How reissues of his records cost him royalties
summary: He recounts handing over scores, a lost letter promising royalties from Prestige, a collector's cleaned-up tape, and being swindled, like Jelly.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: See, Joe was such a friend of mine, I never thought he would do a dipsy-doodle...
That's the same story we hear over and over again, Foots.

Yes. I guess I picked it up from Jelly Roll. I was just so happy to be recording... And then another guy that was... How can I put it? He was a fan of mine. He collected the records, and he's the one that got the idea of putting it on an album. He took it and got as much of the surface noise... See, when we recorded, we didn't record on tape. We recorded on that (?). So he got the idea of putting them on tape. He took as much surface noise out of them as he could, and made it hi-fi. And that I was supposed to get royalties from. Because in my contract, if it ever was produced any other way besides a single record, I was supposed to get royalties.

And another mistake I made, I didn't copy the arrangements. But that was the early days of copying. But I could have just made another copy of the arrangement before I turned it over to him. But I was naive. I turned the score and the arrangements over to him -- but trusting

him. Then he wrote me a letter saying I was going to get the royalties... When the deal came to put the things on Prestige, he wrote me a letter and said I would get my royalties direct from the recording company. I met him one day, and I had misplaced the letter, being down at that darn place on Eighth Avenue... I should have took the letter and put it in my safe, because that was like a contract. And when I checked... I met him one day and brought it to his attention; then he said he never said it -- knowing that I didn't pay no attention to the letter. But that was my fault.
No. He passed on a year or two ago. A lot of times... I found out later he swindled a lot of guys. Otis Blackwell, the guy who wrote all them songs for...
Yeah. I think he swindled him. Because I remember when Otis was writing all them tunes.
Everybody was swindling everybody then. Yeah, the Black guy was on the low end of the totem pole.

And see, I was just so happy. He had given me my break to record. And I really did him a favor. Because see, I knew all the musicians, which he didn't know, and all the musicians who recorded, they did it on account
of knowing me! They didn't do it on account of... And then, too, the ban had just lifted, so everybody was happy to record. Because they hadn't made no money for a year.
